children: Editor’s note: The story has been updated to include comments from political leaders.
The
Federal Aviation Administration
lifted a nationwide ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, nearly five hours after telecommunications failures at air traffic facilities halted departures with more than 3,500 aircraft airborne.
Overloaded Legacy Switches Blamed for FAA Outage
Transportation Secretary
Sean Duffy
said radar and communications became unstable at 3:36 p.m. ET at terminal radar approach control facilities (TRACONs) and en route centers.

"Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data," Duffy said at a news conference, citing the FAA’s analog telecom network. He said upgraded IP-based switches did not fail. "It’s the old hardware that went down."
No Cyberattack Evidence; Duffy Seeks $50 Billion
Homeland Security Secretary
Markwayne Mullin
said officials have seen "zero evidence" of a cyberattack and no link to Thursday’s Microsoft Corp.
email outage, though he did not fully rule it out.

Duffy also asked Congress for $50 billion on top of the $12.5 billion approved in last year’s budget law. "This is an emergency," he said. He warned, "You will have more of these," without full funding.

When asked whether the disruption could cascade into Thanksgiving travel, Duffy said he expects the system to be "back up and operational" as Thanksgiving travel peaks, though he acknowledged it will take time to clear the backlog.
The FAA said it tested its systems before clearing flights to resume. It urged passengers to contact their airlines for updates.

The safety of the flying public is always the FAA’s highest priority. The FAA lifted the ground stop and some flight departures are resuming. Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable.…
Nationwide ground stops are rare. The
, when a contractor unintentionally deleted files tied to a pilot safety system, and before that only after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Political Leaders React to Nationwide Flight Disruption
Former Rep.
Marjorie Taylor Greene

(R-Ga.) cited the ground stop in a post criticizing President Donald Trump. She said he has engaged in "nonstop war mongering for a war that America is against," and that "everyone is rightfully very concerned."

In a later post, Greene criticized the $50 billion funding request, calling it a "shakedown so we can fly safely." She said the administration spends on a White House ballroom and "gaudy gold" décor, and she mocked the call for more money.
$50 billion dollar shakedown so we can fly safely.
But wasting money on a ballroom, gaudy gold all over the WH, building some terrifying Arc filled with weapons, and bombing Iran is totally fine with Trump’s admin.
But fork over more money you pathetic peasants!
How about 🖕🖕🖕
California Gov.
Gavin Newsom
(D) said in an X post that Secretary of State
Marco Rubio
was "defending North Korea" while travelers were "stuck at the airport this Friday night."
Don’t worry, America, while you’re stuck at the airport this Friday night, Marco Rubio is defending North Korea.
Rep.
Nick Langworthy

(R-N.Y.), chairman of the Aviation Safety Caucus, said he was relieved public safety was not compromised. In his X post, he said the outage still caused "enormous inconvenience, stress for travelers and their families."
Langworthy said Congress can no longer afford to delay modernizing air traffic control. He called for transparency from the FAA and its contractors and cited a "yet-to-be-determined economic impact."
Sen.
Jacky Rosen
(D-Nev.) said systems this critical "cannot fail" and called for an investigation.

What happened today was unacceptable. We need to always ensure the safety of the traveling public, and at the same time, systems that are this critical cannot fail. We must investigate what exactly happened here and make sure it never happens again.
